summary.text: A 50-year-old male patient, whose mother had bipolar affective disorder, whose father was a heavy drinker and whose two sisters had depression diagnoses, had behavioral changes with marked isolation due to fearing other people and poor school performance since the age of 13. At age 45 he was afraid to leave home and thought he would be killed. He was first diagnosed with schizophrenia at a hospital in Lima and was treated with olanzapine 5 mg/day, with irregular intake.

At age 49 he began to live alone. He did not care about personal hygiene or basic needs, began giving away his belongings, persisted with ideas of police persecution, could not sleep for several nights and was very anxious. At a hospital in Chiclayo he was treated with olanzapine 10 mg/day and clonazepam 2 mg/day and showed some improvement.

Three months before admission to our unit he moved to Lima with his son and started working in the cleaning area of a school. He stopped taking olanzapine and clonazepam after fifteen days of treatment. Twenty days before admission he refused to eat and said the food was rotten as he was. He was taken to a psychiatric hospital in Lima, where he was treated with fluoxetine 10 mg/day and quetiapine 50 mg/day and showed no improvement.

Seven days before admission he said that he was already dead, his stomach did not work, his liver was decomposed, his brain was paralyzed and his face lacked blood. Four days before admission his relatives took him to a psychiatric hospital and schizophrenia was diagnosed again. He remained hospitalized for three days on haloperidol 30 mg/day IM and clonazepam 3 mg/day without improvement; his family decided to bring him to the emergency room of our hospital before being admitted to the service of General Psychiatry.

Examination found scaly scalp lesions, generalized rigidity, short step gait, a pharaonic position, imperative auditory hallucinations and delusions of nonexistence, immortality and condemnation. Vitamin B12 was 190 pg/mL and Dimer-D 1.45 μg/ml; upper endoscopy showed esophagitis Los Angeles A and brain CT showed no alterations. The proposed diagnoses were schizophrenia, gastroesophageal reflux disease with esophagitis, and seborrheic dermatitis.

Treatment with aripiprazole 30 mg/day was started, with a decision to start clonazepam 2 mg/day. He was significantly improved after two weeks of treatment, with diminished delusions and improved emotional resonance, and said that he was no longer dead. He was discharged after four weeks of hospitalization. The authors state that he follows the criteria of Cotard type I because no depressive symptoms became evident.

article_limitations: Caption-layer visual status not_inspected; the single figure image is reviewed in visual.json.
Figure 1 is a theoretical-model diagram from the literature and Table 1 lists disorders reported in the literature; neither is patient data.

Only explicit lead clauses (Since the age of 13, At age 45, At age 49, and the stated days or months before admission to our unit) are assigned as times; other narrative sentences carry no time, and no calendar dates are stated.
Discussion sentences are used only where they literally say our patient; the unspecified list of phenomena and the plural statement about patients are quarantined as review_only.
Diagnoses described as proposed stay provisional; Cotard syndrome is not among the proposed diagnoses of the case section although the abstract and introduction say the patient developed it.
The hospitals, the three day hospitalization, our unit and the service of General Psychiatry are not identified with each other in the source.
